title: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit
description: Brute force to optimized: restarting tracking for every start versus a sliding window maintained by two monotonic deques (max and min).

sections.title: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit

content.title: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given an array of integers nums and an integer limit, return the length of the LONGEST non-empty contiguous subarray such that the absolute difference between ANY two elements within it is at most limit (equivalently, the subarray's maximum minus its minimum is at most limit).

blocks.caption: A sliding window, tracked by TWO monotonic deques (one for the current max, one for the current min), directly maintains the window's validity as it expands

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of integers nums, and an integer limit"],["Output","The length of the longest subarray whose max minus min is <= limit"],["Goal","Find this length in a single linear pass, tracking the window's max/min efficiently as it slides"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 10^5; 1 <= nums[i] <= 10^9; 0 <= limit <= 10^9"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Absolute difference between ANY two elements\" is equivalent to \"max minus min\"","A sliding window that needs FAST access to its current maximum AND minimum as it expands and shrinks"],["The window must efficiently support removing elements from the LEFT as it shrinks","A monotonic DEQUE (double-ended queue), which supports O(1) removal from both ends while maintaining sorted order at the front"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

The constraint "absolute difference between any two elements <= limit" is exactly equivalent to "the subarray's maximum value minus its minimum value <= limit," since the maximum possible absolute difference within any set of numbers is always between its largest and smallest members.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Widest Acceptable Range of Temperatures in a Rolling Weather Log
blocks.text: Imagine tracking a rolling window of recent temperature readings, wanting the LONGEST stretch where the highest and lowest readings within it never differ by more than a set tolerance. As new readings arrive, the window grows; but the moment the current highest minus current lowest exceeds the tolerance, the window must shrink from the OLDEST end until it becomes valid again. Two "running record" trackers, one for the current max, one for the current min, need to update efficiently as the window both grows and shrinks.

blocks.caption: Two monotonic deques track the window's current max and min at their fronts; when their difference exceeds the limit, the window shrinks from the left until valid again

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [10,1,2,4,7,2], limit = 5

blocks.content: {"headers":["Window","Max","Min","Valid?","Why"],"rows":[["[10]","10","10","Yes","A single element trivially has 0 difference"],["[10,1]","10","1","No (diff=9>5)","Shrink: window becomes [1]"],["[1,2,4,7]","7","1","No (diff=6>5)","Not quite valid"],["[2,4,7,2]","7","2","Yes (diff=5<=5)","A valid window of length 4"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: 4, achieved by the subarray [2,4,7,2] (max 7, min 2, difference 5, exactly at the limit)
5. How Should We Think?

Before recomputing the window's max and min from scratch every time it changes (expensive), notice that TWO monotonic deques, one tracking candidates for the max, one for the min, can be maintained incrementally as the window both grows (on the right) and shrinks (on the left).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: "Max minus min <= limit" needs FAST, UP-TO-DATE access to both the window's current maximum and minimum as it changes; recomputing either from scratch on every step would be too slow.

Observation 2: A monotonic DECREASING deque of indices (values decrease from front to back) always has the window's CURRENT MAXIMUM at its front, since any earlier, smaller value already got popped when a later, bigger value arrived.

Observation 3: Symmetrically, a monotonic INCREASING deque always has the window's CURRENT MINIMUM at its front.

Observation 4: As the window expands (right pointer moves), both deques are updated by popping from the BACK (removing now-irrelevant, dominated values) before pushing the new index, keeping each deque's monotonic property intact.

Observation 5: When the max-min difference (both deques' front values) exceeds the limit, the window must shrink from the LEFT; if the element being removed happens to be exactly the deque's current front (the current max or min), it must also be removed from that deque.

This is the classic sliding window with TWO monotonic deques technique: one deque tracks the window's current maximum, one tracks its current minimum, both maintained incrementally as the window grows and shrinks.
6. Brute Force Solution
For each starting index, extend the subarray rightward one element at a time, tracking the running max and min, stopping as soon as the window becomes invalid.
Step by step algorithm

items: For each starting index i, extend the window (index j from i onward), updating the running max and min at each step.
The moment max - min exceeds limit, stop extending from this starting point (any longer window starting here would also be invalid); otherwise, update the best length found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Tracking the running max/min incrementally as the window extends avoids rescanning the whole window at every step.

Breaking out of the inner loop the moment the window becomes invalid is a valid pruning, since any FURTHER extension from the same start would only ever include MORE values, never fewer, so it cannot become valid again.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly finds the longest valid subarray, since every possible starting point is directly checked, extending until invalid.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: O(n^2) does not scale to the problem's constraints (up to 10^5 elements); a sliding window with two monotonic deques resolves the identical question in O(n).
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force restarts tracking from scratch for every starting point. Instead, maintain a single sliding window (never restarting), tracked by two monotonic deques: one decreasing (for the max), one increasing (for the min). As the window expands, update both deques by popping dominated values from the back before pushing the new index. Whenever max - min exceeds the limit, shrink the window from the left, also popping from either deque's FRONT if the removed element was that deque's current extreme.

Maintain maxDeque (decreasing) and minDeque (increasing), plus a left pointer. For each right index: update both deques (pop dominated values from the back, then push right). While nums[maxDeque.front] - nums[minDeque.front] > limit: increment left, and pop from the FRONT of either deque if its current front index is now outside the window (< left). Update the best length as right - left + 1.
9. Optimized Solution
Maintain a sliding window tracked by two monotonic deques (one for the current max, one for the current min), shrinking from the left whenever the window becomes invalid.
Dry run for nums = [8,2,4,7], limit = 4 (state shown AFTER each right index is fully processed, including any shrinking)

blocks.content: {"headers":["right (val)","maxDeque","minDeque","max, min","Shrink needed?","Window / best"],"rows":[["0 (8)","[0]","[0]","8, 8","No (diff=0<=4)","[0,0] len=1, best=1"],["1 (2)","[1]","[1]","2, 2","Yes: left becomes 1, popping maxDeque's now-stale front (index 0)","[1,1] len=1, best=1"],["2 (4)","[2]","[1,2]","4, 2","No (diff=2<=4)","[1,2] len=2, best=2"],["3 (7)","[3]","[2,3]","7, 2","Yes: left becomes 2, popping minDeque's now-stale front (index 1)","[2,3] len=2, best=2"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The maximum valid window length found is 2, matching the expected result.

codes.python:
from collections import deque

def longest_subarray(nums, limit):
    max_deque = deque()                                                    # DECREASING deque of indices: front is always the window's max
    min_deque = deque()                                                    # INCREASING deque of indices: front is always the window's min
    left = 0
    best = 0
    for right, val in enumerate(nums):
        while max_deque and nums[max_deque[-1]] <= val:                    # maintain decreasing order: pop anything <= the new value
            max_deque.pop()
        max_deque.append(right)
        while min_deque and nums[min_deque[-1]] >= val:                    # maintain increasing order: pop anything >= the new value
            min_deque.pop()
        min_deque.append(right)

        while nums[max_deque[0]] - nums[min_deque[0]] > limit:             # window invalid: shrink from the LEFT
            left += 1
            if max_deque[0] < left:
                max_deque.popleft()
            if min_deque[0] < left:
                min_deque.popleft()

        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(longest_subarray([8, 2, 4, 7], 4))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n): each index is pushed onto each deque exactly once and popped at most once (from either end) across the entire algorithm.
Space: O(n), for the two deques in the worst case.
Why This Works

A monotonic decreasing deque's front is always the current window's maximum, since any value that gets DOMINATED (a later, bigger value appears) is immediately popped from the back, and any value that falls OUT of the window (from the left) is popped from the front. The symmetric argument holds for the increasing deque and the window's minimum. Since both deques always accurately reflect the CURRENT window's extremes, checking their fronts directly (no rescanning) correctly determines validity at every step, and shrinking the window exactly when needed maintains the invariant that the window is always as large as currently possible.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A new value arrives (window expands right)","Both deques are updated: dominated back entries popped, then the new index pushed"],["The window becomes invalid (max - min > limit)","The window shrinks from the left; if the removed index was a deque's current front, that deque's front is also popped"],["The window is valid","Its length (right - left + 1) is compared against the best length found so far"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Both deques store INDICES (not values), so that checking "is this index now outside the window" during shrinking is a simple index comparison.

The shrinking while loop (not a single if) correctly handles cases where multiple left-shrinks might be needed before the window becomes valid again, though in practice usually only one shrink per new right-expansion is needed.

Popping from a deque's FRONT only happens during shrinking (when an element leaves the window on the left); popping from the BACK only happens during expansion (when a new element dominates older ones).

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (restart tracking for every start index)","O(n^2)","O(1) extra","Correct, but repeats overlapping work across different starting points"],["Optimized (sliding window, two monotonic deques)","O(n)","O(n)","Maintains the window's max and min incrementally, never restarting"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

When a sliding window needs FAST access to both its current maximum AND minimum as it both grows and shrinks, TWO monotonic deques (one decreasing for the max, one increasing for the min) maintain both incrementally in O(n) total, avoiding any need to rescan the window.
Common mistakes

items: Using a single deque or a naive running max/min variable, which cannot correctly "un-see" a value once it leaves the window from the left.
Forgetting to check and pop from a deque's FRONT during shrinking, leaving stale (out-of-window) indices that would give an incorrect max or min.
Confusing which side to pop from during expansion (the BACK, for dominated values) versus shrinking (the FRONT, for out-of-window values).

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A single-element array","Trivially valid (max equals min), so the answer is 1"],["limit = 0","Only subarrays of entirely IDENTICAL values are valid, since even a difference of 1 would violate the limit"],["All elements within limit of each other (the whole array is valid)","The window never needs to shrink, and the answer is the full array length"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly stating "max minus min is equivalent to the maximum absolute difference between any two elements" up front simplifies the problem's framing immediately.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Sliding window needing BOTH the current max and min efficiently" points directly to maintaining TWO monotonic deques in parallel.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How does this compare to Sliding Window Maximum (a single monotonic deque)? This problem needs the SAME technique applied TWICE in parallel, once for max and once for min, since both extremes matter for the validity check here.

How would you adapt this if the constraint were on the SUM (not the max-min range) of the window instead? A completely different technique (a simple running sum with a sliding window, no deques needed) would apply, since sum does not require tracking extremes.
What is the amortized cost per element, and why? O(1) amortized, since each index is pushed onto each deque exactly once and popped (from either end) at most once, across the ENTIRE algorithm run.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A direct extension of the single monotonic deque technique from Sliding Window Maximum elsewhere in this category, here maintaining TWO such deques in parallel to track both the window's max and min simultaneously.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (sliding window, two monotonic deques): O(n) time, O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Sliding window with two monotonic deques (max and min)
Core Idea: A decreasing deque tracks the window's current max at its front; an increasing deque tracks the current min; the window shrinks from the left whenever their difference exceeds the limit
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: "Absolute difference between any two elements <= limit" is exactly equivalent to "max - min <= limit," letting two monotonic deques track both extremes efficiently
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Two deques (decreasing=max, increasing=min); expand right, pop dominated backs; while max-min>limit, shrink left, pop stale fronts
